newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish priest charged over anti-Semitic remarks.
newsitem.headline: Polish priest charged over anti-Semitic remarks.

text.p: Polish prosecutors said on Wednesday they had charged a prominent right-wing priest over anti-Semitic remarks he made during a sermon in 1995.

Priest Henryk Jankowski from a parish in the northern city of Gdansk, a former ally of previous president Lech Walesa, compared the Jewish star of David with the communist hammer and sickle and the Nazi swastika.

"Father Jankowski is alleged to have violated the criminal law article...which deals with insulting and humiliating persons of other nationalities," the Gdansk prosecutors' office spokeswoman Maria Jezowska-Kamirska said.
The sermon was attended by Walesa, who lost a race for his second term as president later in 1995 to ex-commmunist Aleksander Kwasniewski.
Walesa was at that time reproached for failing to instantly condemn Jankowski's words, which he said he had not heard. He later issued a statement condemning anti-Semitism.

Jankowski, who was a prominent supporter of the Solidarity union in its pre-1989 fight against communist rule, also said the Polish people should not allow those who owed secret allegiance to Israel or Russia to remain in government.
The probe, prompted by complaints from Polish Jewish groups, will continue until prosecutors decide whether to press the charges with a court or discontinue the case.
Jankowski, who could face up to three years in prison if convicted, said he felt repressed by the charges, which showed there was no freedom of speech in Poland.
"It is a return to a communist totalitarianism," he told reporters in the Baltic port city. "As a Polish citizen I feel persecuted by the Jewish minority."
In 1995, the Polish Roman Catholic Church distanced itself from Jankowski's statements.

"This is a lack of responsibility for one's words, and a destruction of that which has been achieved through long efforts in mutual relations between the Church and Judaism," the Episcopate's secretary, Bishop Tadeusz Pieronek, said.

Jankowski's remarks about Jews declaring their allegiances appeared to echo assertions among some rightist Poles that Jews, now a tiny minority in Poland, exercise secret influence over governments and the economy.

Most of Poland's 3.5 million Jews were murdered by Nazi occupation forces during World War Two. Thousands of survivors left in subsequent waves of emigration, notably during an anti-Jewish campaign mounted by a nationalist faction of the ruling Communist Party in 1968.
